target.title: LiRA: Learning Visual Speech Representations from Audio through Self-supervision

read.pdf: Tables 1–2 and captions/text for Figs. 1–4 reviewed in text.txt; standalone PDF/graphics not supplied

entries.text: LiRA's central idea is to use acoustic features as the self-supervised target for learning visual speech representations.
entries.condition: Pretext training uses unlabelled visual speech and audio-derived PASE+ features.
entries.quote: Speciﬁcally, we train a ResNet+Conformer model to predict acoustic features from unlabelled visual speech.

entries.text: The authors present cross-modal prediction as an underexplored way to obtain visual representations, with audio serving as the training objective.
entries.condition: Motivation and novelty framing in the introduction.

entries.text: The target is the frozen PASE+ encoder's acoustic feature sequence; training minimizes L1 distance from predicted embeddings.
entries.condition: PASE+ is pretrained and frozen; features are extracted from waveform audio.
entries.quote: To train the model, we apply an L1 loss between the generated embeddings and the features extracted from the pre-trained (frozen) PASE+ model, as shown in Fig. 1.

entries.text: Mouth ROIs are obtained from facial landmarks and geometrically normalized to a neutral reference frame.
entries.condition: dlib landmark detection; fixed mouth bounding box; ROI size 96 × 96 pixels; reference-frame normalization removes rotation and size differences.

entries.text: Visual augmentation uses random horizontal flips and random crops for training; evaluation uses a centered crop.
entries.unit: flip probability; crop pixels; mixup weight
entries.condition: Word-level mixup weight is 0.4; test crop is centered rather than random.

entries.text: LRS3 is the unlabelled pretraining corpus and contains TED-talk utterances.
entries.condition: LRS3 is used for self-supervised pretraining; utterance durations vary and are longer than LRS2 on average.

entries.text: The paper states that LRS3 has no speaker overlap between its train and test sets.
entries.condition: This statement concerns LRS3; the paper does not say which LRS3 partitions were used for pretraining.

entries.text: LRW consists of short labelled word clips from a fixed vocabulary and multiple speakers/backgrounds.
entries.unit: utterances; seconds per utterance; hours; vocabulary words
entries.condition: BBC programs; hundreds of speakers and varied backgrounds/head poses; evaluation is word-level recognition.

entries.text: LRS2 contains transcribed utterances of varying duration and a large, mostly unconstrained vocabulary.
entries.condition: BBC programs; sentence-level recognition; the paper later reports 222 hours of labelled LRS2 training data.

entries.text: The pretext network uses a 3D front end, ResNet-18 spatial encoder, Conformer temporal encoder, and MLP projection head.
entries.unit: Conformer blocks; PASE+ and visual frames per second
entries.condition: PASE+ frame features are averaged over time to match the visual frame rate; the Conformer dimensions are dff=2048, nhead=4, dq=dk=dv=256.

entries.text: Pretext training uses Adam with the Noam learning-rate schedule and a fixed warm-up period.
entries.condition: Pretraining batch size 32 on LRS3; no random seed or run count is given.

entries.text: Pretraining randomly samples a one-second segment per clip and drops clips shorter than one second.
entries.unit: second sampled per clip; minimum clip duration in seconds
entries.condition: The sampled video segment is the pretext model input; the paper does not state a sampling seed.

entries.text: Word-level supervised training uses an MS-TCN and 500-way linear classifier, optimized with cross-entropy and AdamW.
entries.unit: classes; epochs; batch size; initial learning rate; weight decay
entries.condition: AdamW β1=0.9, β2=0.999, ε=10−8; word-level mixup is described separately in t5.

entries.text: Sentence-level recognition uses a hybrid CTC/attention architecture, trained with CTC and cross-entropy losses.
entries.unit: attention blocks; epochs; batch size; initial learning rate; warm-up steps
entries.condition: Adam β1=0.9, β2=0.98, ε=10−9; transformer decoder; training utterances longer than 600 frames are excluded (t17).

entries.text: Sentence-level beam search uses a beam size of 20.
entries.condition: The paper does not report the beam-search scoring weights or the language-model fusion weight.

entries.text: Decoding applies a Transformer language model trained on LRS2, LRS3, and LibriSpeech.
entries.condition: The paper does not specify the corpus partitions used for LM training or confirm which held-out text was excluded.
entries.quote: During decoding, we also apply a transformer-based language model trained on LRS2, LRS3, and Librispeech 960h [25] (16.2 million words in total).

entries.text: The authors exclude long training utterances because of GPU memory limits.
entries.unit: frames; utterances longer than this are excluded
entries.condition: The exclusion is stated for sentence-level downstream training.

entries.text: The paper evaluates supervised-from-scratch, frozen-feature, and fine-tuned initializations for both word- and sentence-level lip-reading.
entries.condition: Fine-tuned models initialize the encoder with weights learned on the self-supervised pretext task.

entries.text: The authors claim fine-tuning consistently beats training from scratch and is especially helpful with small labelled datasets.
entries.condition: Claim is based on LRW and LRS2 downstream experiments; see t20–t38 for reported results.

entries.text: ResNet + BLSTM [37] supervised LRW word recognition result reported for comparison.
entries.condition: LRW word-level, 500-word vocabulary; no language model for this classification score; the prior system's test split, speakers/sessions, training data, and seeds are not restated.

entries.quote: LiRA-Frozen Self-supervised 83.1

entries.condition: LRW word-level, 500-word vocabulary; pretrained on unlabelled LRS3 and fine-tuned on labelled LRW; benchmark split, speakers/sessions, and seeds are not stated; no language model is used for classification.
entries.quote: LiRA-FineTuned Self-supervised 88.1

entries.text: LiRA-Supervised accuracy when trained with one percent of the labelled LRW training set.
entries.condition: LRW word-level, 500-word vocabulary; 1% of the labelled training set (LRW training duration 165 hours); model trained from scratch; test split, speakers/sessions, and seeds are unspecified; no language model.
entries.quote: In the extreme case, where only 1 % of the labelled training data is used, LiRA-Supervised achieves an accuracy of 3.6 %.

entries.text: LiRA-FineTuned accuracy when trained with one percent of the labelled LRW training set.
entries.condition: LRW word-level, 500-word vocabulary; 1% of the labelled training set (LRW training duration 165 hours); initialized from LRS3; test split, speakers/sessions, and seeds are unspecified; no language model.
entries.quote: In contrast, we obtain 24.5 % accuracy when LiRA- FineTuned is trained using the same amount of data.

entries.text: The authors report that fine-tuning improves full-data LRW accuracy over their supervised baseline.
entries.unit: percentage-point absolute improvement, as claimed in prose
entries.condition: Full labelled LRW training set, 500-word vocabulary; test split, speakers/sessions, and seeds are unspecified; no language model. Prose claims 0.8 points, while Table 1's 88.1% versus 87.4% differs by 0.7 points (inference).
entries.quote: We also show that LiRA-FineTuned provides an absolute improvement of 0.8 % in accuracy over LiRA-Supervised when both are trained on full LRW.

entries.text: Hyb. CTC/Att. [29] supervised LRS2 sentence-recognition WER reported for comparison.
entries.condition: LRS2 sentence-level recognition, vocabulary over 40,000 words; prior test split, speakers/sessions, labelled/external data, seeds, and decoding/LM conditions are not restated in Table 2.

entries.text: Conv-seq2seq [43] supervised LRS2 sentence-recognition WER reported for comparison.
entries.condition: LRS2 sentence-level recognition, vocabulary over 40,000 words; prior test split, speakers/sessions, labelled/external data, seeds, and decoding/LM conditions are not restated in Table 2.

entries.condition: LRS2 sentence-level recognition, vocabulary over 40,000 words; prior test split, speakers/sessions, labelled/external data, seeds, and decoding/LM conditions are not restated in Table 2.

entries.condition: LRS2 sentence-level recognition, vocabulary over 40,000 words; curriculum starts from 11% of labelled training clips under 155 frames, then uses the full set; test split, speakers/sessions, and seeds are unspecified; decoding uses beam 20 and the stated Transformer LM (t15–t16).
entries.quote: LiRA-Supervised [16] Supervised (CL) 39.1

entries.text: LiRA-FineTuned reaches the reported best LRS2 sentence-level WER in Table 2.
entries.condition: LRS2 sentence-level recognition, vocabulary over 40,000 words; pretrained on unlabelled LRS3 and fine-tuned with labelled LRS2; test split, speakers/sessions, and seeds are unspecified; decoding uses beam 20 and the stated Transformer LM (t15–t16). No external labelled dataset is used for model training.
entries.quote: LiRA-FineTuned Self-supervised 38.8

entries.text: The authors report a 9.5-point absolute WER improvement over the previous best LRS2 result.
entries.condition: LRS2 sentence-level recognition, vocabulary over 40,000 words; LiRA-FineTuned 38.8% versus previous best 48.3% WER; benchmark split, speakers/sessions, and seeds unspecified; LiRA decoding uses beam 20 and the stated Transformer LM (t15–t16).
entries.quote: We also observe that it leads to a 9.5 % absolute im- provement compared to the previous state-of-the-art model [1], as reported in Table 2.

entries.text: LiRA is reported to outperform the previous LRS2 WER using substantially less labelled training data.
entries.unit: data reduction factor; hours and percent of LRS2; comparator labelled hours
entries.condition: LRS2 sentence-level recognition, vocabulary over 40,000 words; 76 labelled hours (36% of LRS2) for LiRA versus 1,362 hours from MVLRS, LRS2, and LRS3; benchmark split, speakers/sessions, seeds, and prior-system decoding/LM are unspecified.
entries.quote: 76 hours (36 % of LRS2) vs 1 362 hours (MVLRS, LRS2, and LRS3).

entries.text: The authors claim their method outperforms prior self-supervised LRW systems and achieves state of the art on LRS2.
entries.condition: LRW claim is specifically against other self-supervised methods; Table 1 also lists a supervised result at 88.4% (t23). LRS2 claim is qualified by no external labelled training datasets.
entries.quote: We show that our approach signiﬁcantly outperforms other self-supervised methods on the Lip Reading in the Wild (LRW) dataset

entries.text: The authors say the self-supervised initialization consistently beats scratch training, including with larger labelled training sets.
entries.condition: Downstream comparison is between LiRA-FineTuned and LiRA-Supervised.

entries.text: The authors state that fine-tuned features can support both word-level and sentence-level lip-reading.
entries.condition: Evaluated by feature extraction and fine-tuning on LRW and LRS2.

entries.text: The authors report that predicting MFCC features performed worse than predicting PASE+ features.
entries.condition: This is a qualitative comparison; no MFCC result or metric is given.
entries.quote: We would also like to mention that we have also experimented with predicting MFCC features but the results were worse than predicting PASE+ features.

entries.text: The authors say scratch training on LRS2 is difficult to optimize and degrades as the training set grows beyond the stated fraction, likely because of long utterances.
entries.condition: Applies to LiRA-Supervised sentence-level training from scratch; the authors introduce curriculum learning to address it.
entries.quote: The performance becomes worse and worse as the training set increases beyond 18 % of the total amount of labelled data.

entries.text: The authors suggest extending the approach to emotion and speaker recognition as future work.
entries.condition: Proposed directions only; not evaluated in this paper.

entries.text: The paper does not define the LRW train/validation/test partition, test-set size, or the test speakers and their overlap with training speakers.
entries.condition: Applies to the LRW word-level evaluation; the paper gives aggregate corpus size and speaker diversity but no evaluation split protocol.

entries.text: The paper does not define the LRS2 evaluation partition, test-set size, or test-speaker overlap with the training data.
entries.condition: The LRS3 non-overlap statement in t7 does not establish the LRS2 evaluation split or speaker overlap.

entries.text: No random seeds, number of independent runs, or across-run variability are reported for pretraining or downstream evaluation.
entries.condition: The paper gives optimizer settings and some random augmentation but no seed/repetition protocol, standard deviations, or confidence intervals.
entries.quote: We optimise our model using Adam (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98, ϵ = 10−9) combined with the Noam scheduler [39] (25 000 warm-up steps).

entries.text: The paper does not identify a validation split or specify checkpoint selection and hyperparameter-selection criteria.
entries.condition: Training recipes state epochs and learning rates but do not describe validation data or model-selection rules.

entries.text: Input ROI geometry is normalized, but pixel-value normalization and normalization of predicted/acoustic feature targets are not specified.
entries.condition: The stated normalization is landmark-based rotation/size normalization against a neutral frame; no mean/variance or equivalent feature normalization is described.

entries.text: The paper does not report a chance-level or other trivial baseline for the 500-class LRW accuracy task.
entries.condition: No chance accuracy is calculated here; the paper states the vocabulary size but gives no chance-baseline result.

entries.text: The WER scoring normalization and tokenization rules are not described.
entries.condition: No case, punctuation, tokenization, or reference-normalization procedure is specified for LRS2 WER.

entries.text: Although the paper states that LRS3 is used for self-supervised pretraining, it does not identify the LRS3 partition or partitions used.
entries.condition: It is therefore not possible from the paper to determine whether any particular LRS3 held-out partition was excluded from pretraining.
entries.quote: In this work, we use an unlabelled version of Lip Reading Sen- tences 3 (LRS3) for pre-training and evaluate the performance of speech representations on LRW and LRS2.

entries.text: The language-model training sentence lists corpora but does not specify corpus partitions or held-out-text exclusion.
entries.condition: LM data are stated as LRS2, LRS3, and LibriSpeech; exact partitions and any overlap with evaluation references are unspecified.

entries.text: No statistical test or uncertainty estimate is supplied to support the prose claim of significant superiority.
entries.condition: Results are presented as point estimates; significance tests, confidence intervals, and standard deviations are not reported.
entries.quote: We show that our approach signiﬁcantly outperforms other self-supervised methods on the Lip Reading in the Wild (LRW) dataset

entries.text: The paper specifies beam size but not language-model fusion/scoring coefficients or other decoding details needed to reproduce sentence recognition.
entries.condition: Beam size is 20; decoding also applies the language model described in t16.

entries.text: The pretext task uses unlabelled LRS3; downstream evaluation is on labelled LRW and LRS2.
entries.condition: No manual labels are used for the described pretraining objective; downstream recognition uses dataset labels/transcriptions.

entries.text: The paper gives the labelled training-data durations used for LRW and LRS2 data-fraction plots.
entries.unit: hours of labelled training data; LRW; LRS2
entries.condition: The data-fraction experiments are on LRW word recognition and LRS2 sentence recognition, respectively.

entries.text: Word-level lip-reading produces a class prediction from a linear classifier following the MS-TCN.
entries.condition: A 500-way classifier is specified for LRW in t13; sentence-level output is decoded using the CTC/attention model in t14–t16.

entries.text: The authors claim state-of-the-art sentence-level LRS2 performance using only a fraction of the labelled data.

entries.text: The paper does not report recording-session counts or train/test session overlap for the LRW and LRS2 evaluations.
entries.condition: The datasets are described as coming from BBC programs, but session-level partitioning or overlap is not specified; see also the split/speaker gaps in t48–t49.

entries.text: The authors observe that deeper pretext layers generally perform worse for downstream feature classification and suggest reduced transfer generalization as a possible explanation.
entries.condition: Layerwise frozen-feature evaluation on LRW; the paper gives a plotted curve in Fig. 3 and reports 83.1% for the final ResNet-18 layer in text/table.

questions.q: What is the self-supervised signal, and how is it used to initialize lip-reading models?
questions.answer: LiRA predicts frozen PASE+ acoustic features from unlabelled visual speech, then evaluates frozen features and pretrained initialization on word- and sentence-level lip-reading.

questions.q: What are the headline LRW and LRS2 results, and what data conditions accompany them?
questions.answer: The paper reports 88.1% LRW accuracy and 38.8% LRS2 WER; the exact benchmark partitions and several protocol details are not specified.

questions.q: What qualifications should accompany the superiority and data-efficiency claims?
questions.answer: The comparison table includes a higher supervised LRW score; the LRS2 gain uses a language model and the paper omits run variability, split definitions, and decoding fusion weights.

questions.q: Which limitations do the authors explicitly report?
questions.answer: MFCC targets were worse than PASE+; long LRS2 training clips were excluded for memory limits, and scratch training degraded on longer utterances as more data were added.

questions.q: Does the paper qualify its LRS2 state-of-the-art claim and how large does it call the fine-tuning gain over curriculum learning? (writer, targeted grep of Sec. 4.2 and Sec. 1)
questions.answer: Yes: 'when no external labelled datasets are used for training'; the gain over curriculum learning is called 'a small improvement'; Afouras et al. are credited with ASR labels that still rely on a labelled-data ASR.

questions.q: LipSound 2019 (isca-qu19-lipsound): target of prediction, use of transcripts, how used for lip reading, dataset and speaker protocol (writer grep after the reader passed 20 min)
questions.answer: Video to mel spectrogram, trained without transcripts; a DeepSpeech 2 back end reads the generated spectrogram; GRID speaker-dependent, 0.843% CER / 2.525% WER.
